title: A systematic survey for hypervelocity runaways from thermonuclear supernovae
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, submitted to OJAp. Data at https://doi.org/10.22002/aff3x-28035
summary: The explosion of a white dwarf (WD) in a close binary can launch a surviving runaway star at velocities of $\gtrsim 1000\, \rm km\,s^{-1}$. Such runaways provide a direct probe of thermonuclear supernovae (SNe) in double-degenerate binaries. Several candidate runaways are known, but their evolutionary states and the demographics of the broader population are uncertain. To enable robust population inference, we carry out a systematic survey for hypervelocity runaways with a simple selection function, selecting candidates based on large Gaia-inferred tangential velocities and blue colors. We classify 100% of the resulting 92 candidates using a combination of spectroscopic follow-up and archival data. The search yields ten suspected D$^6$ stars and three LP 40-365 stars. Three D$^6$ stars are new discoveries, including two hot ($T_{\rm eff} > 50,000$ K) objects and one cool ($T_{\rm eff}\approx 7,000$ K) object. We forward-model our survey under several proposed D$^6$ star evolutionary models, coupling each to a Galactic model and the survey selection function. No single model reproduces the observed diversity of D$^6$ stars, which likely reflects a range of remnant masses, ages, and heating mechanisms. Models in which runaway companions are heated by SN shocks alone are too faint and short-lived to explain most of the observed sample, while fully reheated models are too luminous and long-lived. Models with intermediate heating, as occurs in some simulations of violent mergers and partially disrupted remnants, best match the observed magnitude, distance, and kinematic-age distributions. The inferred D$^6$ star birth rate is model dependent, but the models that best match the observed population require rates of only a few percent of the Galactic SN Ia rate, perhaps implying that most SNe Ia result from WD binaries in which both components explode.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey of hypervelocity runaway stars from white dwarf explosions in double-degenerate binaries identified 10 D^6 stars and 3 LP 40-365 stars. Forward modeling shows that intermediate heating models best explain the observed diversity, implying these runaways represent only a few percent of Galactic SN Ia events.
AI.motivation: To understand the demographics and evolutionary states of hypervelocity runaway stars launched by white dwarf explosions in close binaries, and to infer the nature of thermonuclear supernovae in double-degenerate systems.
AI.method: Systematic survey using Gaia tangential velocities and blue colors to select 92 candidates, classified via spectroscopic follow-up and archival data. Forward-modeling was applied with different D^6 star evolutionary models coupled to a Galactic model and survey selection function.
AI.result: Ten suspected D^6 stars (three new discoveries: two hot >50,000 K, one cool ~7,000 K) and three LP 40-365 stars. No single evolutionary model reproduces the observed diversity. Intermediate heating models best match observations; shock-heated models are too faint/short-lived, fully reheated models too luminous/long-lived.
AI.conclusion: The inferred D^6 star birth rate is only a few percent of the Galactic SN Ia rate, suggesting most SNe Ia likely result from WD binaries where both components explode.

title: Summary of the First Year of the Space Weather Around Young Suns Program: 900 Hours of Low-frequency Radio and Optical Data Dedicated to Young, Solar-type Stars
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to ApJ
summary: The Space Weather Around Young Suns (SWAYS) program was introduced in \citet{Davis2025} as a multi-wavelength monitoring program for studying the activity and particle environments of nearby, young, solar-type stars. The SWAYS program currently includes the Owens Valley Radio Observatory Long Wavelength Array (OVRO-LWA) operating between 13--87\,MHz to search for stellar equivalents of solar type~II and III bursts, which are associated with bulk plasma motion in the corona and interplanetary medium. These observations are accompanied by simultaneous photometric data from the high-precision, optical instrument Flarescope to identify associated flare events. These two instruments have collectively acquired nearly 900\,hr of data with $\approx70\%$ overlap between November 2023--June 2024, dedicated to six stars. Here, we present the results of this first season of the SWAYS observing campaign, which include a superflare from the star EK~Draconis with no accompanying low-frequency particle-flux signal. The novelty of the coordination at these specific parts of the spectrum allow us to uniquely evaluate the conditions that may have inhibited a radio detection. We find that the exceptionally hot, dense coronae of incredibly active stars may not be conducive to the development of the instabilities required for type~II and III bursts, or else inspire new expectations for when we should expect to observe a signal relative to the time of the flare. This may represent the plasma-density complement to the magnetospheric limitations to observing space-weather signatures at low frequencies.

AI.tldr: The SWAYS program's first season monitored six young solar-type stars for ~900 hours using OVRO-LWA (radio) and Flarescope (optical), finding a superflare on EK Draconis with no associated low-frequency radio emission, suggesting that hot, dense coronae of active stars may inhibit type II/III burst mechanisms.
AI.motivation: To study the space weather environments (activity and particle emissions) of young, solar-type stars through coordinated multi-wavelength monitoring, searching for stellar analogs of solar type II and III radio bursts associated with coronal and interplanetary plasma motions.
AI.method: Coordinated observations using OVRO-LWA (13–87 MHz) for low-frequency radio emission and Flarescope for high-precision optical photometry, collectively acquiring ~900 hours of data with ~70% overlap between November 2023–June 2024 across six target stars.
AI.result: Detection of a superflare from EK Draconis with no accompanying low-frequency particle-flux signal, indicating that the hot, dense coronae of highly active stars may suppress the instabilities needed for type II and III radio bursts, representing a plasma-density complement to previously known magnetospheric limitations.
AI.conclusion: The exceptional coronal conditions of incredibly active stars may not favor the development of instabilities required for type II/III bursts, or may shift expectations for when radio signals should appear relative to flare timing; this highlights plasma-density limitations to observing space-weather signatures at low frequencies.

title: Empirical colour--effective temperature relations in the SDSS system from IRFM temperatures of GALAH and APOGEE stars
comment: 12 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Reliable estimates of stellar effective temperature ($T_{\mathrm {eff}}$) are fundamental to stellar population studies and Galactic astrophysics. However, the majority of stars observed in modern large-scale photometric surveys lack spectroscopic measurements, making empirical colour--$T_{\mathrm {eff}}$ relations essential tools. In this work, we present updated empirical colour--$T_{\mathrm {eff}}$ calibrations based on Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) $ugriz$ photometry combined with 2MASS $JHK_{\mathrm s}$ data. Effective temperatures are determined on a homogeneous InfraRed Flux Method (IRFM) scale using a combined sample of 3902 GALAH and 2535 APOGEE stars with high-quality photometry and well-characterised atmospheric parameters. Using this dataset, we establish empirical relations between $T_{\mathrm {eff}}$ and colour indices constructed from SDSS and 2MASS combinations. We provide both colour--metallicity--$T_{\mathrm {eff}}$ and colour--$T_{\mathrm {eff}}$ relations for dwarfs and giants. The calibrations are derived using low-order polynomial models with iterative $3σ$ clipping. Their performance depends on the adopted colour index, with long-baseline colours such as $(g-K_{\mathrm s})_0$ and $(g-z)_0$ achieving internal precisions of $\sim$30--50~K. Comparisons with previous calibrations show general agreement, with differences attributable to sample selection, photometric zero-points, and functional form. The resulting relations provide a homogeneous and internally consistent framework for estimating $T_{\mathrm {eff}}$ from SDSS and 2MASS photometry alone, and are well suited for application to large photometric surveys lacking spectroscopic information.

AI.tldr: This paper presents updated empirical colour–Teff calibrations using SDSS ugriz and 2MASS JHKs photometry, based on 3902 GALAH and 2535 APOGEE stars with homogeneous IRFM temperatures. It provides colour–metallicity–Teff and colour–Teff relations for dwarfs and giants, achieving ~30–50 K precision for long-baseline colours, suitable for photometric surveys without spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Reliable Teff estimates are fundamental for stellar population and Galactic astrophysics, but most stars in large photometric surveys lack spectroscopic measurements, necessitating empirical colour–Teff relations.
AI.method: Empirical relations are derived using SDSS ugriz + 2MASS JHKs photometry from 3902 GALAH and 2535 APOGEE stars with homogeneous IRFM Teff scales, using low-order polynomial models with iterative 3σ clipping.
AI.result: Long-baseline colours like (g−Ks)0 and (g−z)0 achieve ~30–50 K internal precision. Results agree with previous calibrations, with differences due to sample selection, photometric zero-points, and functional form.
AI.conclusion: The relations provide a homogeneous, internally consistent framework for estimating Teff from SDSS and 2MASS photometry alone, well-suited for large photometric surveys lacking spectroscopic information.

title: Protostellar Outflows at the EarliesT Stages (POETS). IX. Magnetohydrodynamic disk winds traced by SO and SO$_2$ in luminous protostars
comment: 12 pages with 5 figures (plus Appendix of 4 pages), accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We investigate two massive young stellar objects (YSOs), IRAS21078+5211 and G035.02+0.35, where evidence for magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk winds (DWs) has been obtained at scales of 10-100 au through measurements of the 22GHz water maser velocity distribution within the Protostellar Outflows at the EarliesT Stages (POETS) survey. We employ IRAM Northern Extended Millimeter Array and archival Atacama Large Millimeter Array observations of IRAS21078+5211 and G035.02+0.35, respectively, to study kinematics and physical conditions of the corresponding protostellar winds on scales of 100-1000 au using the same molecular tracers. In IRAS21078+5211, the emissions of several molecules, particularly SO, SO2, CH3CN and CH3OH, are distributed along the axis of the radio jet, and present a LSR velocity (Vlsr) gradient transversal to the jet axis. Position-velocity (PV) plots of the SO lines show patterns consistent with Keplerian rotation. The SO2 emission comes from high velocity gas flowing close to the jet axis, while CH3CN and CH3OH present larger radial extension than the S-bearing species. In G035.02+0.35, the same molecules are instead distributed along the major axis of the rotating disk, and their Vlsr gradients consistently trace the disk rotation. The corresponding PV plots present Keplerian profiles. SO is the only molecular species whose emission extends well outside the disk. In both YSOs, the spatial and velocity distributions of SO are consistent with a rotating wind magneto-centrifugally launched from the YSO disk. The comparison with models of molecule formation and excitation in shocks indicates that the different radial extension of the molecular species observed in the protostellar wind of IRAS21078+5211, as well as the lack of molecules, except SO, in the G035.02+0.35's wind, can be explained in terms of a radially extended MHD DW, rather than a compact X-wind.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates two massive young stellar objects (IRAS21078+5211 and G035.02+0.35) using molecular line observations at 100-1000 au scales to study protostellar winds. In IRAS21078+5211, SO, SO2, CH3CN, and CH3OH trace a rotating wind with Keplerian rotation patterns. In G035.02+0.35, only SO extends into the wind region while other molecules trace the disk. Both sources show SO distributions consistent with magneto-centrifugally launched rotating winds. The findings favor a radially extended MHD disk wind over a compact X-wind scenario.
AI.motivation: To study the kinematics and physical conditions of protostellar winds on scales of 100-1000 au in two massive YSOs where MHD disk winds have already been detected at smaller scales (10-100 au) via 22 GHz water maser observations.
AI.method: Observations using IRAM Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) for IRAS21078+5211 and archival ALMA data for G035.02+0.35, employing multiple molecular tracers (SO, SO2, CH3CN, CH3OH) to analyze velocity distributions, position-velocity diagrams, and spatial extent of emission relative to jet and disk axes.
AI.result: In IRAS21078+5211, molecules are distributed along the radio jet axis with transversal velocity gradients and Keplerian PV profiles; in G035.02+0.35, molecules trace disk rotation except SO which extends outside the disk. The radial extent of molecular species differs between the two sources, consistent with predictions of a radially extended MHD DW model.
AI.conclusion: The observed molecular distributions and kinematics in both YSOs are consistent with rotating, magneto-centrifugally launched disk winds. The differing molecular extent (particularly SO) supports a radially extended MHD disk wind rather than a compact X-wind model.

title: pop-cosmos: Disentangling galaxy properties from observables using data-driven approaches
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures, comments welcome
summary: The physical processes that shape a galaxy's spectrum are strongly degenerate in observations, obscuring which processes act independently. Leveraging the pop-cosmos generative galaxy population model, we investigate how many independent degrees of freedom the rest-frame optical SED contains. We use a $β$-variational autoencoder (VAE) to compress a 16-parameter stellar population synthesis (SPS) description into a disentangled latent representation interpreted through mutual information (MI). We find that five independent dimensions suffice, corresponding to stellar mass, recent star formation, dust, and two -- not the three or four assumed by standard nebular models -- degrees of freedom in the ionization state of the gas. Stellar metallicity and stellar age are not among these primary drivers; their spectral effects are distributed across the others rather than independently encoded. By tying each dimension to specific spectral features, this decomposition breaks the star-formation--dust--metallicity degeneracies that limit broadband photometry, and recovers the physical conditions of the gas more cleanly than the line-ratio diagnostics in standard use.

AI.tldr: Using a β-VAE on the pop-cosmos model, this paper finds that galaxy rest-frame optical SEDs have only five independent physical degrees of freedom: stellar mass, recent star formation, dust, and two (not three or four) ionization state parameters. Stellar metallicity and age are not independent but distributed across other axes.
AI.motivation: To resolve degeneracies in galaxy spectra that obscure which physical processes act independently, by determining the true number of independent degrees of freedom in rest-frame optical SEDs.
AI.method: A β-variational autoencoder (β-VAE) compresses a 16-parameter SPS description into a disentangled latent space, evaluated via mutual information (MI) to identify independent dimensions.
AI.result: Five independent dimensions are sufficient: stellar mass, recent star formation, dust, and two (not the standard three or four) ionization state degrees of freedom. Stellar metallicity and age are not independently encoded.
AI.conclusion: This decomposition breaks key degeneracies (star-formation–dust–metallicity) and recovers gas physical conditions more cleanly than standard line-ratio diagnostics.

title: Building three-dimensional giant stellar models for common envelope simulations
comment: It will be submitted in two days to allow for comments (including missing references)
summary: We build a three-dimensional (3D) red supergiant (RSG) stellar model for common envelope evolution (CEE) simulations by transporting a 1D stellar model to a 3D numerical grid, mimicking core nuclear power by depositing energy to an inner shell, and mimicking stellar emission by cooling grid cells with densities below the photospheric density. We do not relax the model; rather, we let it perform its natural pulsation. We find that when we mimic photospheric emission by cooling low-density grid cells, the oscillations slowly decay on a time scale much longer than in the absence of photospheric cooling. When we mimic both nuclear energy production, by depositing the stellar luminosity in an inner shell above the inert core of the stellar model, and the photospheric cooling, the oscillations do not decay and their amplitude slowly increases with time. The main pulsational period is about 1 year, comparable to the stellar dynamical time, suggesting a fundamental radial pulsation mode. The non-spherical structure of the stellar model and rapid low-amplitude temporal variations in the average stellar radius testify to the presence of non-radial oscillation modes on top of the fundamental radial mode. We also obtain vigorous convection, as RSG stars have. We conclude that the best way of preparing a giant star to simulate CEE and grazing-envelope evolution is to deposit energy with the stellar luminosity in an inner shell, and to cool the outer low-density numerical shell. There is no need to relax the model.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a 3D RSG stellar model for CEE simulations by depositing nuclear energy in an inner shell and cooling low-density outer cells to mimic photospheric emission, finding that this combination sustains natural pulsations (∼1-year period) and convection without needing model relaxation.
AI.motivation: To construct realistic 3D red supergiant stellar models suitable for common envelope evolution simulations, avoiding artificial relaxation while preserving natural stellar pulsation and convection.
AI.method: Transport a 1D stellar model to 3D grid; mimic core nuclear power by depositing energy to an inner shell; mimic photospheric emission by cooling low-density grid cells below photospheric density; let the model pulsate naturally without relaxation.
AI.result: Photospheric cooling alone causes slow oscillation decay; adding inner-shell energy deposition sustains oscillations with slowly increasing amplitude. Main pulsational period ∼1 year (fundamental radial mode). Non-radial modes and vigorous convection are also observed.
AI.conclusion: The optimal preparation method for giant stars in CEE and grazing-envelope simulations is to deposit stellar luminosity in an inner shell and cool the outer low-density shell, with no need for model relaxation.

title: Comparison and verification methods to trace interaction-driven disturbances in galaxies
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 17 pages
summary: Low surface brightness tidal debris around galaxies, such as tails, streams, and shells, together with other interaction-driven morphological disturbances, serve as valuable indicators of past or ongoing galaxy mergers. With the growing data volume from surveys like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), automated detection methods are essential. This paper evaluates the performance of two automated methods, a Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) model and the Concentration-Asymmetry-Smoothness (CAS) parameter method, in tracing interaction-driven disturbances and merger signatures, with visual classification used as the benchmark. Visual classification yields a high-confidence disturbance fraction of 25.1 +/- 1.5% in our sample and serves as the reference standard for assessing the completeness and precision of the automated approaches. Visual classification is affected by galaxy distance and image resolution, which limit the detectability of faint low surface brightness structures. The SSL model achieves high recall (0.86 +/- 0.04) and low contamination (0.2) by retraining only its linear classifier on a small labelled dataset, making it suitable for identifying a broad set of disturbed systems, including faint tidal debris and other interaction-driven morphological disturbances, thereby providing a more complete census of merger-related features. The CAS method, using the traditional threshold A > 0.35, shows higher precision (0.77) but lower recall (0.20), indicating a conservative approach that captures cleaner but less complete samples. Visual classification and the SSL model show a significant positive correlation between stellar mass and disturbance fraction, while the CAS method exhibits a much weaker trend.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates automated methods (SSL model and CAS parameters) for detecting low-surface-brightness tidal debris and merger signatures in galaxies, using visual classification as a benchmark. SSL achieves high recall (0.86) and low contamination (0.2), while CAS shows higher precision (0.77) but low recall (0.20). Visual classification yields 25.1% disturbance fraction.
AI.motivation: With growing data volumes from surveys like LSST, automated detection of low-surface-brightness tidal debris (tails, streams, shells) and merger signatures is essential for studying galaxy interactions at scale.
AI.method: Compared a Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) model (retraining only its linear classifier on a small labelled dataset) and the Concentration-Asymmetry-Smoothness (CAS) parameter method (using traditional threshold A > 0.35) against visual classification as the benchmark reference standard.
AI.result: SSL model: recall 0.86±0.04, contamination 0.2; CAS method: precision 0.77, recall 0.20; Visual classification: 25.1±1.5% disturbance fraction. Stellar mass–disturbance correlation significant for visual and SSL, weaker for CAS.
AI.conclusion: SSL is suitable for a broad, complete census of merger-related features including faint tidal debris, while CAS provides cleaner but less complete samples; visual classification remains the benchmark but is limited by distance and resolution.

title: Oscillations of red giant stars with magnetic damping in the core. II. Mixed mode visibilities on the red-giant branch
comment: accepted by A&A
summary: Mode visibilities can be estimated from observed power spectra or from theory by making assumptions about the damping processes occurring in the star. However, a quantitative comparison between the two approaches was so far not feasible due to observational biases. The biases arise from the fact that in observations, the power spectrum is divided into frequency segments in which modes of a certain spherical degree are expected to dominate. In this work, we used synthetic power spectra to calculate the visibility as it has been done in observations and compare it with published observed visibilities to quantify the influence of the biases. We find that, taking the biases into account, the observed spatial response of the dipole modes is 1.47, which is closer to the theoretical value than previous estimates. In particular, we predict that the normalized dipole mode visibility of late red-giant branch (RGB) stars might be overestimated by up to 20% in published observations. For stars with depressed dipole modes, we find that the normalized dipole mode visibilities estimated in observational studies might be overestimated by 20% throughout their entire evolution on the RGB. The quadrupole mode visibility, on the other hand, appears to be largely unaffected by the biases, expect on the late RGB. In addition, we investigated the evolution of the visibility and detectability of the mixed mode signature while testing different prescriptions for the energy loss caused by a strong internal magnetic field in the stellar core. We argue that taking into account the inner turning point of the g-mode cavity could allow a portion of the mode energy to be preserved when interacting with a strong magnetic field. We further show that such partial dissipation allows the mixed mode signature to be both present or absent in the observable power spectra, which is consistent with observations.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies observational biases in mode visibility estimates from power spectra, showing that dipole mode visibilities for red-giant branch stars may be overestimated by up to 20% in published observations, while quadrupole modes are largely unaffected. It also explores how internal magnetic fields affect mixed mode detectability, proposing partial energy dissipation at the g-mode cavity's inner turning point.
AI.motivation: To enable quantitative comparison between observed and theoretical mode visibilities by accounting for observational biases arising from segmenting power spectra by spherical degree, which previously prevented such comparison.
AI.method: Synthetic power spectra were used to calculate visibilities as done in observations, then compared with published observed visibilities to quantify bias effects. Different prescriptions for energy loss due to strong internal magnetic fields were tested to investigate mixed mode signature detectability.
AI.result: After accounting for biases, observed dipole mode spatial response is 1.47 (closer to theory). Normalized dipole mode visibilities may be overestimated by up to 20% for late RGB stars and throughout the RGB for stars with depressed dipole modes. Quadrupole modes are largely unaffected except on the late RGB. Partial dissipation at the g-mode cavity's inner turning point can explain the presence or absence of mixed mode signatures in power spectra.
AI.conclusion: Observational biases significantly affect dipole mode visibility estimates for RGB stars; accounting for these biases brings observed values closer to theoretical predictions. A model of partial magnetic energy dissipation at the g-mode cavity's inner turning point can reconcile the observed variability of mixed mode signatures.

title: Spiral arms across cosmic time: JWST measurements of the pitch angles of spiral galaxies at $z<3.5$
comment: Accepted to ApJ, 14 pages
summary: The properties of spiral galaxies in the early universe remain poorly studied and, as such, little is known about their nature and evolution. We use JWST data to measure the pitch angles of spiral galaxies across cosmic time. Our sample consists of 593 spiral galaxies with stellar masses ($M_*$) greater than $10^{10} M_\odot$ up to $z \sim 3.5$, drawn from the CEERS and JADES surveys. Spiral galaxies are identified by fine-tuning a Zoobot deep-learning model. We use SpArcFiRe to identify spiral arms and measure their pitch angles. We find no significant redshift evolution in the average pitch angle across the full sample. However, in the most massive systems (log$(M_*/M_\odot)=11-12$), spiral arms slightly wind up with time. We show that at $z>1.25$, pitch angle does not correlate with some key internal galaxy properties (stellar mass, bulge mass, disk mass, specific star formation rate [sSFR]). In contrast, at $z<1.25$, pitch angle shows a weak but statistically significant negative correlation with stellar mass, bulge mass, and disk mass, and a positive correlation with sSFR at $z<0.75$. We also find no dependence of pitch angle on the tidal strength applied by nearby companions. These results indicate a transition epoch at $z\sim1$: above this redshift, spiral structures appear to be primarily locally driven and not correlated with global galaxy properties; and below this redshift, spiral arms are regulated by global gravitational potential, consistent with the predictions of the density wave theory.

AI.tldr: Using JWST data of 593 spiral galaxies up to z~3.5, the study finds no redshift evolution in average pitch angle overall, but massive systems show winding over time. A transition at z~1 is identified: above z~1, pitch angles don't correlate with galaxy properties (locally driven); below z~1, correlations emerge with stellar/bulge/disk mass and sSFR, consistent with density wave theory.
AI.motivation: Spiral galaxy properties in the early universe remain poorly understood, motivating the need to study their nature and evolution across cosmic time using high-redshift observations.
AI.method: 593 spiral galaxies (M* > 10^10 M⊙, z up to ~3.5) from CEERS and JADES surveys. Zoobot deep-learning model fine-tuned for identification, SpArcFiRe for arm detection and pitch angle measurement. Analysis of correlations with stellar mass, bulge mass, disk mass, sSFR, and tidal interactions.
AI.result: No significant redshift evolution of average pitch angle across full sample. Most massive systems (log M*/M⊙=11-12) show slight winding over time. At z>1.25, no correlation with galaxy properties. At z<1.25, weak negative correlations with stellar/bulge/disk mass; positive correlation with sSFR at z<0.75. No dependence on tidal strength of companions.
AI.conclusion: A transition epoch exists at z~1: above this redshift, spiral structures are locally driven, uncorrelated with global properties; below z~1, spiral arms are regulated by global gravitational potential, supporting density wave theory predictions.

title: Near-core magnetic field strengths inferred from gravity modes in intermediate-mass stars
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A on June 10th 2026
summary: In this work, we derive upper limits for the strength of the near-core magnetic field in intermediate-mass stars, since high-order g-modes can be fully suppressed by a critical magnetic field. Both poloidal and toroidal components of the magnetic field are included. We examine how the upper limits on magnetic field strengths are affected by the degree and azimuthal order of the oscillations, as well as the magnetic field configuration. We consider two gamma-Doradus stars hosting high-order g-modes and an evolved delta-Scuti star with mixed modes, all with prior mode identification from observations. We determine the best structural model from their stellar parameters through grid-based modeling with MESA. Frequencies for the best models are extracted using GYRE and matched to the observed modes. The critical magnetic fields for all calculated frequencies in our models are obtained from the Dedalus code, from which we can infer an upper limit on the near-core field strength. We find an upper limit on the near-core radial field strength of Br ~ 130 kG and Br ~ 13 kG, assuming a dipole field configuration, for the two gamma-Doradus stars KIC 3127996 and KIC 5876187, respectively. For 44 Tau, analysis of mixed modes yields a field strength of Br ~ 1771 kG. Different magnetic field configurations and mode degrees lead to different estimates. The results for the radial component of the magnetic field in the main sequence gamma-Doradus stars are consistent with estimates of magnetic field strengths in red giant stars that assume an internal field generated by a core dynamo, although the stronger of the two inferred magnetic fields may require some enhancement by a fossil field. The toroidal component does not affect g-modes significantly and is required to be more than 200 times stronger than the radial component to suppress g-modes. (abridged for arXiv)

AI.tldr: This paper derives upper limits on near-core magnetic field strengths in intermediate-mass stars using observed g-modes and mixed modes. Upper limits of ~130 kG and ~13 kG are found for two γ-Doradus stars (dipole field), and ~1771 kG for the δ-Scuti star 44 Tau. The toroidal component must be >200× stronger than the radial component to suppress g-modes.
AI.motivation: To constrain the strength of near-core magnetic fields in intermediate-mass stars, since high-order g-modes can be suppressed by a critical magnetic field, and such internal fields are poorly understood observationally.
AI.method: Grid-based modeling with MESA, frequency extraction with GYRE, mode matching to observations, and computation of critical magnetic fields using the Dedalus code for both poloidal and toroidal field components.
AI.result: Upper limits: Br ~130 kG (KIC 3127996), Br ~13 kG (KIC 5876187) for γ-Doradus stars with dipole configuration; Br ~1771 kG for 44 Tau from mixed modes. Toroidal component must exceed radial by factor >200 to suppress g-modes.
AI.conclusion: Results for main-sequence γ-Doradus stars are consistent with core dynamo field estimates in red giants; the stronger field may require fossil field enhancement. Toroidal fields have negligible effect on g-modes.

title: Phase-dependent magnetic coherence in the turbulent interstellar medium
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: Magnetic fields permeate the multiphase interstellar medium (ISM), yet their phase-dependent structure remains poorly constrained by observations. Dust polarization and \ion{H}{1} emission together offer complementary probes of the plane-of-sky magnetic field and cold neutral medium (CNM) gas structure, respectively. Recent observational work has shown that in the diffuse ISM, the dust polarization fraction correlates positively with the CNM mass fraction ($f_{\rm CNM}$) but not with total \ion{H}{1} column density, suggesting a phase-dependent magnetic field geometry. Here, we use extremely high-resolution ($2048^3$) simulations of the turbulent, magnetized, multiphase ISM to investigate the physical origin of this trend. By constructing synthetic \ion{H}{1} and dust polarization maps, we directly compare our simulations to the observational results of \citet{Lei:2024}. We recover a positive $f_{\rm CNM}$-polarization correlation most clearly for sightlines intersecting fewer than $\sim$20 discrete CNM clouds, while the trend becomes weak or intermittent for larger cloud counts, consistent with the expectation that high-Galactic-latitude sightlines contain relatively few independent cold structures. We show that this correlation reflects genuine phase-dependent magnetic structure: CNM clouds tend to be elongated along the local magnetic field and, when normalized by column density, exhibit lower magnetic disorder than the warm neutral medium (WNM). We further demonstrate that apparent discrepancies between simulation- and observation-based measures of magnetic disorder arise from whether disorder is quantified per unit path length or per unit mass. Our results support a picture in which CNM structures host relatively ordered magnetic fields, producing higher polarization fractions along CNM-dominated sightlines in the diffuse ISM.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution (2048^3) simulations of turbulent, magnetized, multiphase ISM, this study recovers the observed positive correlation between CNM mass fraction and dust polarization fraction, showing that CNM clouds are elongated along magnetic fields with lower magnetic disorder than WNM, and resolves discrepancies in magnetic disorder quantification between simulations and observations.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origin of the observed positive correlation between dust polarization fraction and CNM mass fraction in the diffuse ISM, and to investigate phase-dependent magnetic field geometry that remains poorly constrained by observations.
AI.method: Extremely high-resolution (2048^3) simulations of turbulent, magnetized, multiphase ISM; construction of synthetic HI and dust polarization maps; direct comparison with observational results from Lei+2024; analysis of cloud count dependence and magnetic disorder quantification.
AI.result: Positive f_CNM-polarization correlation is recovered most clearly for sightlines with fewer than ~20 discrete CNM clouds; CNM clouds are elongated along local magnetic fields and exhibit lower magnetic disorder than WNM when normalized by column density; discrepancies between simulation and observation measures arise from whether disorder is quantified per unit path length or per unit mass.
AI.conclusion: CNM structures host relatively ordered magnetic fields, producing higher polarization fractions along CNM-dominated sightlines in the diffuse ISM, supporting a phase-dependent magnetic field geometry picture.

title: Shaping the horizontal branch: The role of envelope mass in the evolution of stripped core-helium-burning stars
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The location of a star along the horizontal branch (HB) during core-helium burning is primarily determined by the amount of mass lost by its progenitor. We investigate the formation and properties of stripped core-helium-burning stars, focusing on how the residual hydrogen-envelope mass ($M_{\mathrm{env}}$) and the timing of envelope removal shape their properties. We used the MESA stellar evolution code to model stars that lose their hydrogen envelopes on the first giant branch. We explored two limiting cases for the timing of stripping, corresponding to the minimum and maximum core masses for helium ignition, for progenitors with initial masses below $\sim$6 $M_{\odot}$ at two metallicities ($Z=0.02$ and $Z=0.004$), while systematically varying $M_{\mathrm{env}}$. As expected, the effective temperature along the HB decreases as $M_{\mathrm{env}}$ increases. We determined the maximum $M_{\mathrm{env}}$ required to avoid subsequent evolution through the thermally pulsing asymptotic giant branch, which ranges from $\sim0.05$ $M_{\odot}$, for low-mass progenitors to $\sim0.30$ $M_{\odot}$ for intermediate-mass progenitors. In low-mass progenitors, early envelope removal triggers a late hot flash, naturally explaining the hottest blue hook stars. In intermediate-mass systems, partial envelope stripping can produce extended pre-HB configurations consistent with puffed-up stripped stars observed in binaries with Be companions. Our post-stripping evolutionary tracks are publicly available for use in binary evolution and population synthesis studies.

AI.tldr: This paper studies stripped core-helium-burning stars, modeling how the residual hydrogen-envelope mass and timing of envelope removal affect their properties along the horizontal branch, with applications to blue hook stars and stripped stars in Be binaries.
AI.motivation: To understand how the residual hydrogen-envelope mass and the timing of envelope stripping determine the properties of stripped core-helium-burning stars, and to provide constraints on envelope masses needed to avoid AGB phase evolution.
AI.method: Used the MESA stellar evolution code to model stars losing hydrogen envelopes on the first giant branch, exploring two limiting cases (minimum and maximum core masses for helium ignition) for progenitors below ~6 M☉ at two metallicities (Z=0.02 and Z=0.004), systematically varying Menv.
AI.result: Effective temperature along the HB decreases with increasing Menv; maximum Menv to avoid thermally pulsing AGB ranges from ~0.05 M☉ (low-mass) to ~0.30 M☉ (intermediate-mass); early envelope removal in low-mass progenitors triggers late hot flashes explaining blue hook stars; partial stripping in intermediate-mass systems produces extended pre-HB configurations matching stripped stars in Be binaries.
AI.conclusion: The timing and extent of envelope stripping crucially shape HB star properties, explaining observed blue hook stars and puffed-up stripped stars in binaries; post-stripping evolutionary tracks are publicly released for binary evolution and population synthesis studies.

title: Morphology, sizes, and scatter in a large sample of distant quiescent galaxies
summary: After quenching galaxies keep growing in size across time, as established in the literature up to cosmic noon. In this work, we assemble one of the largest and most comprehensive multi-wavelength photometric sample of massive quenched galaxies at z > 3, counting 137 quiescent candidates within 825 sq.arcmin and redshift 3<z<7 across the well-studied extragalactic JWST fields. We model their surface brightness distribution across 5 bands mapping their UV-to-NIR rest-frame wavelength with Sersic profiles, and derive their sizes, concentrations, and ellipticities. The size-mass relation is consistent with previous studies. Size decreases with increasing redshift, in agreement with previous studies and extending them up to z_spec=4.9. The intrinsic scatter of the mass-size relation has no relevant dependence on the redshift and the filter used. Our multi-wavelength modeling reveals that size decreases with increasing observed wavelength, and the wavelength gradient decreases with increasing stellar mass. This result proves that in the NIR-bands massive elliptical galaxies appear more compact. The Sersic index does not show significant dependence on wavelength, independently of the stellar mass. Following a forward/backward Bayesian fit analysis to assess the significance of several parameters in predicting the size of our sample, we do not identify any significant secondary dependence of the size on axis ratio q, Sersic index n, UVJ-colors, and environment. The combination of stellar mass and redshift is sufficient to predict the size of quiescent galaxies at z>3, albeit with a large scatter. This suggests that the commonly used parameters of a Sersic distribution cannot explain the large intrinsic scatter around the stellar mass-size relation, suggesting that other physical quantities need to be taken into account to break the degeneracy between evolution paths across the galaxy population.

AI.tldr: This paper studies 137 massive quenched galaxies at z>3 across JWST fields, finding that their size decreases with increasing redshift and observed wavelength, with stellar mass and redshift being sufficient to predict size, while Sersic parameters and other factors fail to explain the large intrinsic scatter around the mass-size relation.
AI.motivation: To understand the size evolution of massive quenched galaxies at z>3, extending previous studies to higher redshifts and characterizing the multi-wavelength structural properties of these galaxies.
AI.method: Assembled a multi-wavelength photometric sample of 137 quiescent galaxy candidates at 3<z<7 across JWST fields; modeled surface brightness with Sersic profiles in 5 bands; performed Bayesian forward/backward fitting to assess secondary dependencies.
AI.result: Size decreases with increasing redshift (up to z_spec=4.9) and with increasing observed wavelength; wavelength gradient decreases with stellar mass; Sersic index shows no wavelength dependence; no significant secondary dependence on axis ratio, Sersic index, UVJ colors, or environment; stellar mass and redshift alone are sufficient to predict size but with large scatter.
AI.conclusion: Common Sersic parameters cannot explain the large intrinsic scatter around the mass-size relation, indicating other physical quantities are needed to break degeneracies between evolution pathways in the quiescent galaxy population at z>3.

title: Three-Phase Evolution of Aspect Ratio in Fast and Slow CMEs from the Sun to 1 AU
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables; Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) undergo significant geometric evolution as they propagate from the Sun to 1 AU, influencing their radial size, expansion, and space weather impact. We investigate the evolution of CME aspect ratio and expansion dynamics for four fast and four slow Earth-directed CMEs. Using multipoint coronagraphic observations with the Graduated Cylindrical Shell (GCS) model and corrected in situ measurements of associated magnetic clouds (MCs) at 1 AU, we track the evolution of aspect ratio from the low-middle corona to interplanetary space. We find that aspect ratio does not remain constant but exhibits a systematic three-phase evolution: a rise phase in the low-middle corona ($\lesssim10$-$15\,R_{\odot}$), a saturation phase at intermediate heights, and then a decline phase in the interplanetary space. The ratio of radial expansion speed to leading-edge speed ($V_{\rm exp}/V_{\rm LE}$) decreases substantially from the corona to 1 AU, indicating a reduction in radial expansion efficiency during interplanetary propagation. The consistent evolution of aspect ratio and $V_{\rm exp}/V_{\rm LE}$ suggests a transition from magnetically dominated expansion in the corona to a regime increasingly controlled by the heliospheric environment. We note that fast CMEs show stronger early expansion and evolve into larger, more radially extended structures, whereas slow CMEs exhibit a more gradual rise and a steeper decline. These results demonstrate that CME geometry evolves significantly during propagation and highlight the need to incorporate aspect ratio evolution in models to improve predictions of CME size, arrival time, and geoeffectiveness.

AI.tldr: This study tracks the aspect ratio evolution of eight Earth-directed CMEs from the corona to 1 AU, revealing a systematic three-phase behavior (rise, saturation, decline) linked to changing expansion dynamics and a transition from magnetically dominated to heliospheric-controlled propagation.
AI.motivation: To understand how CME geometry evolves during propagation and how this affects space weather prediction, specifically the aspect ratio and expansion dynamics that influence radial size, arrival time, and geoeffectiveness.
AI.method: Multipoint coronagraphic observations and the Graduated Cylindrical Shell (GCS) model for the low-middle corona, combined with corrected in situ measurements of magnetic clouds at 1 AU, analyzing four fast and four slow Earth-directed CMEs.
AI.result: Aspect ratio shows a three-phase evolution: rise ($\lesssim 10$-$15 R_\odot$), saturation, then decline. $V_{\rm exp}/V_{\rm LE}$ decreases substantially from corona to 1 AU. Fast CMEs exhibit stronger early expansion and larger radial structures; slow CMEs show a more gradual rise and steeper decline.
AI.conclusion: CME geometry evolves significantly during propagation, transitioning from magnetically dominated to heliospheric-controlled expansion, and models must incorporate aspect ratio evolution to improve predictions of CME size, arrival time, and geoeffectiveness.

title: CRIRES+ reveals the chemistry of the stellar sub-populations in the bulge fossil fragment Liller 1
comment: Accepted for publication on ApJ, 16 pages, 11 figures
summary: In this paper we present the chemical screening of the complex stellar population discovered in the Bulge Fossil Fragment Liller 1. This study is part of the Bulge Cluster Origin (BulCO) survey based on a Large Program at the ESO-VLT with the high resolution spectrograph CRIRES+. The survey is aimed at performing an unprecedented chemical screening of 17 stellar systems orbiting the Milky Way bulge, with the ultimate goal of unveiling their origin and true nature. We measured precise chemical abundances of iron, CNO, iron-peak, $α$- other light-elements, and neutron-capture elements for a sample of 30 red giant branch stars, kinematic members of Liller 1. The presented analysis provides the high-resolution spectroscopic proof of the complex chemistry of this massive stellar system, with multi-metallicity sub-populations of different ages that nicely fits into a self-enrichment scenario. We find no evidence for the Na-O anticorrelation associated with genuine globular clusters; rather the overall abundance trends are similar to those seen in the bulge field and in Terzan 5, providing definitive evidence of an in-situ formation of Liller 1 within the Galactic bulge.

AI.tldr: This paper presents precise chemical abundance measurements of 30 red giant branch stars in Liller 1 using CRIRES+ high-resolution spectroscopy, revealing multi-metallicity sub-populations with different ages consistent with self-enrichment, no Na-O anticorrelation (typical of globular clusters), and abundance trends similar to the bulge field and Terzan 5, confirming Liller 1 formed in-situ within the Galactic bulge.
AI.motivation: To unveil the origin and true nature of Liller 1, a complex stellar population discovered in the Bulge Fossil Fragment, by performing a detailed chemical screening as part of the Bulge Cluster Origin (BulCO) survey.
AI.method: High-resolution spectroscopic observations with CRIRES+ at ESO-VLT, measuring precise chemical abundances of iron, CNO, iron-peak, α-elements, other light elements, and neutron-capture elements for 30 kinematic member red giant branch stars of Liller 1.
AI.result: Liller 1 exhibits multi-metallicity sub-populations of different ages fitting a self-enrichment scenario, lacks the Na-O anticorrelation characteristic of genuine globular clusters, and shows abundance trends similar to the bulge field and Terzan 5.
AI.conclusion: Liller 1 formed in-situ within the Galactic bulge, providing definitive evidence against it being a genuine globular cluster and supporting its classification as a bulge fossil fragment.

title: JADES: the mass-metallicity relation at $z=1-10$. New calibrations, extremely metal-poor galaxies, and chemical diversity
comment: Submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present gas-phase metallicities of star-forming galaxies at $z=1$-10 with deep JWST/NIRSpec spectra from the JADES full data release, Dark Horse, and OASIS programmes. We stack $\sim$1500 medium-resolution spectra, yielding detections of the [OIII]$λ$4363 auroral line down to $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=7.0$ to derive stack-based strong-line calibrations over the metallicity range $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=7.0$-8.7. At a fixed metallicity, our stacks exhibit [OIII]$λ$5007/H$β$ and [OIII]$λ$5007/[OII]$λλ$3726,3729 values generally lower than calibrations based on high-$z$ individual auroral-line emitters, suggesting an observational bias towards higher excitation introduced when requiring auroral line detections in individual spectra. Based on our new calibrations, we obtain canonical mass-metallicity relations (MZRs) at z$=$1-10, identifying a decrease in metallicities from $z\sim0$ to z$\sim$4-10, without significant change in slope. Moreover, we identify 50 promising candidates of extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs) with $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=6.7$-7.3 (1-4\% solar metallicity) at $z=1.2$-9.1. The MZRs of EMPGs are characterised by a large scatter, with those having lower metallicities generally exhibiting lower sSFRs, opposite of what expected from the local Fundamental Metallicity Relation. These results support a stochastic star-formation history involving gas consumption/ejection and metal-poor inflow, strongly affecting metallicities of low-mass galaxies. Furthermore, we identify two Little Red Dots in our EMPG candidates, both exhibiting broad H$α$ and prominent Ly$α$, offering insights into the early black-hole growth in extremely metal-poor environments.

AI.tldr: Using ~1500 stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectra from JADES, Dark Horse, and OASIS, we derive strong-line metallicity calibrations at z=1-10, establish mass-metallicity relations, identify 50 extremely metal-poor galaxy candidates (1-4% solar), and find two Little Red Dots with broad Hα and Lyα in EMPG candidates.
AI.motivation: To derive robust strong-line metallicity calibrations from stacked spectra (rather than individual auroral-line detections) across z=1-10, and to characterize the mass-metallicity relation and extremely metal-poor galaxy population at these redshifts using deep JWST/NIRSpec data.
AI.method: Stacking ~1500 medium-resolution JWST/NIRSpec spectra from JADES, Dark Horse, and OASIS; detecting [OIII]λ4363 down to 12+log(O/H)=7.0; deriving stack-based strong-line calibrations; constructing mass-metallicity relations; identifying EMPG candidates via metallicity cuts.
AI.result: Stack-based calibrations yield lower [OIII]λ5007/Hβ and [OIII]λ5007/[OII] at fixed metallicity vs. individual auroral-line emitters, indicating excitation bias. MZRs show decreasing metallicity from z~0 to z~4-10 with unchanged slope. 50 EMPG candidates identified at 1-4% solar metallicity (z=1.2-9.1), with lower-metallicity ones showing lower sSFR (opposite of local Fundamental Metallicity Relation). Two Little Red Dots with broad Hα and Lyα found in EMPG sample.
AI.conclusion: Individual auroral-line detections are biased towards higher excitation; stacked calibrations are more representative. The anti-correlation between metallicity and sSFR in EMPGs supports stochastic star-formation histories with gas consumption/ejection and metal-poor inflows. Two Little Red Dots in EMPG candidates provide insights into early black-hole growth in extremely metal-poor environments.

title: Imprints of the Neutral Interstellar Medium on Polarized Synchrotron Emission and Faraday Rotation
summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) is a complex, multiphase medium, where disentangling the distribution of gas and magnetic field structure across different phases remains a considerable challenge. Recently, Faraday tomography enabled by broadband polarized radio observations has emerged as a promising probe of 3D ISM gas and magnetic field structures. However, the interpretation of these observations is obscured by our limited understanding of the different ISM components probed by the distinct Faraday depth features. In this work, we present a comprehensive multi-frequency ($\sim$300 MHz - 23 GHz) analysis comparing features in the Faraday-rotated, polarized synchrotron emission and HI structures over the full high-latitude (|b|>30 degrees) diffuse sky. Using measures of HI structure complexity along the line of sight (LOS), we observe enhanced depolarization across synchrotron radio frequencies in regions with high HI complexity characterized by multiple HI velocity components. We also find that the first and second moments of the Faraday depth spectra are linked to the underlying neutral gas structure. These results indicate that regions of the ISM that are dominated by neutral gas could directly contribute a significant portion of the diffuse synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation. These findings establish new observational constraints for Galactic magnetic field models that synthesize multiphase tracers into a single coherent picture.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multi-frequency (300 MHz–23 GHz) analysis comparing Faraday tomography features and HI structures across the high-latitude diffuse sky, finding that regions with complex HI structure show enhanced depolarization and that Faraday depth spectrum moments are linked to neutral gas structure, suggesting neutral gas regions contribute significantly to diffuse synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation.
AI.motivation: The interstellar medium (ISM) is a complex multiphase medium where disentangling gas distribution and magnetic field structure across different phases remains a considerable challenge, and the interpretation of Faraday tomography observations is limited by poor understanding of which ISM components are probed by distinct Faraday depth features.
AI.method: Comprehensive multi-frequency (~300 MHz–23 GHz) analysis comparing Faraday-rotated polarized synchrotron emission and HI structures over the full high-latitude (|b|>30°) diffuse sky, using measures of HI structure complexity along the line of sight.
AI.result: Enhanced depolarization across synchrotron radio frequencies is observed in regions with high HI complexity (multiple HI velocity components). The first and second moments of Faraday depth spectra are linked to underlying neutral gas structure.
AI.conclusion: Regions of the ISM dominated by neutral gas could directly contribute a significant portion of diffuse synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation, establishing new observational constraints for Galactic magnetic field models that synthesize multiphase tracers.

title: Flagging Super-Eddington Candidates among Jetted, γ-Ray-Emitting AGN
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, submitted as a proceedings paper to Physical Science Forum
summary: The quasar Eigenvector-1/Main Sequence (E1/MS) provides a physically motivated empirical framework to organize the spectroscopic diversity of type~1 active galactic nuclei (AGN). In its optical plane, the full width at half maximum of H$β$ and the Fe\,II strength ratio $R_{\mathrm{FeII}}$ define a sequence that is primarily driven by Eddington ratio, with important secondary roles played by black-hole mass, orientation, spectral energy distribution, and chemical enrichment. The E1/MS framework is therefore well suited to identify highly accreting and possibly super-Eddington (SE) sources, usually associated with the extreme Population~A (xA) spectral types. We discuss why E1/MS is a useful tool to search for SE accretors among jetted AGN and, conversely, to place $γ$-ray-detected AGN in the broader context of quasar phenomenology. We summarize two complementary results: (1) some candidate SE accretors show radio properties such as high brightness temperature non-thermal cores or radio lobes} consistent with jet activity; and (2) a subset of low-redshift $γ$-ray narrow-line Seyfert~1 galaxies exhibit optical spectra consistent with xA or borderline-xA classification. We also expand the discussion of recent developments in E1/MS studies, including metallicity trends, the spectral energy distribution of xA quasars, and the role of highly accreting quasars as discovery tools for extreme accretion states, as probes of quasars at the reionization epoch, and as possible cosmological probes.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses how the quasar Eigenvector-1/Main Sequence (E1/MS) framework, particularly extreme Population A (xA) spectral types, can identify highly accreting/super-Eddington sources among jetted AGN and gamma-ray-detected narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, and reviews recent developments including metallicity trends, SEDs, and cosmological applications.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the utility of the E1/MS framework for identifying super-Eddington accretors among jetted AGN and gamma-ray-detected sources, and to place these objects in the broader context of quasar phenomenology.
AI.method: Review and synthesis of E1/MS framework using the optical plane defined by Hβ FWHM and Fe II strength ratio R_FeII, with emphasis on extreme Population A (xA) spectral types as tracers of high Eddington ratio accretion.
AI.result: (1) Candidate SE accretors exhibit jet-related radio properties (high brightness temperature non-thermal cores, radio lobes). (2) A subset of low-redshift gamma-ray narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies show xA or borderline-xA optical spectra.
AI.conclusion: The E1/MS is a powerful tool for identifying super-Eddington accretors among jetted AGN and gamma-ray sources, and highly accreting quasars serve as probes of extreme accretion states, reionization-era quasars, and potential cosmological probes.

title: SDSS-V LVM: Revealing the Physical and Chemical Structure of the Helix Nebula
summary: We present the first spatially contiguous study of the physical and chemical structure of the Helix Nebula (NGC~7293, PNG 036.1-57.1) based on integral-field spectroscopy from the SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM). The wide-field observations provide nearly complete spectroscopic coverage of the nebula, enabling a spaxel-by-spaxel analysis of extinction, electron density and temperature, ionisation structure, and chemical abundances. We reconstruct calibrated datacubes from the LVM row-stacked spectra and measure 41 optical emission lines, including hydrogen, helium, and collisionally excited metal lines. The resulting maps reveal a strongly stratified nebula, with highly ionised gas traced by \heii~concentrated toward the central cavity, low-ionisation material dominating the bright shell, and neutral or transition-zone gas enhanced in the outer regions. The Helix is a low-density object, with typical electron densities of $\sim10^{2}\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, and exhibits a non-uniform temperature structure, with variations of several thousand Kelvin across different ionisation zones. We derive a near-solar oxygen abundance, $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})\simeq8.7$, consistent with spatially complete sampling. The central abundance pattern indicates a significant contribution from unobserved O$^{3+}$, suggesting that apparent abundance variations are primarily driven by ionisation effects rather than true chemical inhomogeneities. We also find evidence for a sulfur deficit of $\sim$1 dex, consistent with the planetary-nebula sulfur anomaly. The helium and nitrogen abundances place the Helix near the classical boundary of Type~I planetary nebulae, suggesting moderate chemical enrichment by its progenitor star.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first spatially contiguous integral-field spectroscopic study of the Helix Nebula using SDSS-V LVM data, revealing a stratified structure with varying ionization, temperature, and density. Chemical abundances are near-solar with evidence of a sulfur deficit and moderate enrichment, positioned near the Type I planetary nebula boundary.
AI.motivation: To provide the first complete, spatially contiguous study of the physical and chemical structure of the Helix Nebula using wide-field integral-field spectroscopy, enabling spaxel-by-spaxel analysis of its properties.
AI.method: SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM) integral-field spectroscopy; reconstruction of calibrated datacubes from row-stacked spectra; measurement of 41 optical emission lines (H, He, and collisionally excited metal lines); spaxel-by-spaxel mapping of extinction, electron density, temperature, ionization structure, and chemical abundances.
AI.result: Strongly stratified nebula: He II concentrated in central cavity, low-ionization gas in bright shell, neutral/transition-zone gas in outer regions. Electron density ~10² cm⁻³. Non-uniform temperature structure with variations of several thousand K. Near-solar O abundance (12+log(O/H)~8.7). Sulfur deficit of ~1 dex (sulfur anomaly). He and N place Helix near Type I PN boundary.
AI.conclusion: Apparent abundance variations are driven by ionization effects (particularly unobserved O³⁺) rather than true chemical inhomogeneities. The Helix Nebula shows moderate chemical enrichment and lies near the classical Type I planetary nebula boundary.

title: Investigating the role of turbulence in the interstellar medium in $z\sim3$ dusty star-forming galaxies using kpc-resolution ALMA dust and gas maps
summary: We present ALMA high-resolution ($\sim$0.25$^{\prime\prime}$/2 kpc) CO(5-4) and CO(4-3) observations of three $z\sim 3$ submillimetre-selected dusty galaxies from the ALESS survey. These data complement existing [sub]-kpc scale ALMA 870$μ$m continuum imaging and JWST NIRCam and MIRI imaging from the ALESS-JWST program, allowing us to trace the molecular gas, dust-obscured star formation, and stellar populations on similar spatial scales. We spectroscopically confirm that two of the sources lie at the same redshift and are likely interacting. We find that the molecular-gas distribution broadly follows the dusty star-forming structures seen in the 870$μ$m dust continuum imaging, but that the gas reservoirs are significantly more extended than the dust emission with a spatial extent comparable to the rest-frame near-infrared stellar emission. By modeling the kinematics for the two highest signal-to-noise sources, we find that the galaxies are well-fit by rotating disc models with high ratios of ordered to random motion ($V_{\rm{max}}/\overlineσ=5\pm1$ and $6\pm1$), although smaller-scale kinematic deviations cannot be ruled out at the current sensitivity and spatial resolution. Finally, utilizing the high-resolution 870$μ$m dust continuum and CO data, we investigate star-formation scaling relations on kpc-scales in these high-redshift galaxies. Assuming a constant CO-to-H$_{2}$ conversion factor and excitation ratio, we find that the data are offset from theoretical star-formation relation predictions that do not take turbulence into account, but consistent with gravo-turbulent models, thereby suggesting that turbulence plays a central role in regulating star formation at high redshift.

AI.tldr: This paper presents ALMA CO(5-4) and CO(4-3) observations of three z~3 dusty galaxies from the ALESS survey, resolving molecular gas on ~2 kpc scales. Two sources are spectroscopically confirmed at the same redshift (likely interacting). Molecular gas is more extended than dust continuum but comparable to stellar emission. Kinematic modeling reveals rotating discs with high ordered-to-random motion (V_max/σ~5-6). kpc-scale star-formation scaling relations are offset from turbulence-free predictions but consistent with gravo-turbulent models, suggesting turbulence regulates high-redshift star formation.
AI.motivation: To understand the spatial distribution, kinematics, and star-formation regulation mechanisms of molecular gas in high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies, bridging the gap between dust-obscured star formation and stellar populations on sub-kpc scales.
AI.method: ALMA high-resolution (~0.25″/2 kpc) CO(5-4) and CO(4-3) imaging of three z~3 ALESS submillimeter galaxies, combined with existing ALMA 870μm continuum and JWST NIRCam/MIRI data. Kinematic modeling with rotating disc models; kpc-scale star-formation scaling relation analysis using CO and dust continuum.
AI.result: (1) Two sources are at the same redshift and likely interacting. (2) Molecular gas is more extended than 870μm dust emission, with spatial extent comparable to rest-frame near-IR stellar emission. (3) Galaxies are well-fit by rotating disc models with V_max/σ = 5±1 and 6±1. (4) kpc-scale star-formation relations are offset from turbulence-free theoretical predictions but consistent with gravo-turbulent models.
AI.conclusion: Turbulence plays a central role in regulating star formation at high redshift; standard turbulence-free star-formation relations fail to reproduce the observed kpc-scale data, while gravo-turbulent models succeed.

title: Geometry and Kinematics of Molecular Cloud Substructures in the Second Galactic Quadrant
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, accepted by Acta Astronomica Sinica
summary: We analyze the geometry and kinematics of substructures within molecular clouds identified in an unbiased catalog from the MWISP survey. These substructures are defined as spatially connected regions enclosed by the 20% peak-integrated-intensity contour of each cloud. After applying selection criteria on voxel size and excluding structures truncated by map boundaries, we construct a sample and quantify their projected morphology using the projected scale ratio $R=Δb/(Δl\cdot\cos b)$. This ratio essentially measures $\tanθ$ where $θ$ is the plane-of-sky angle of an elongated filament relative to the Galactic plane. The resulting sample exhibits a median $R=0.96$, indicating a slight but systematic preference for elongation along Galactic longitude. This tendency becomes more pronounced at larger spatial scales. We further investigate the relative orientations among the structural major axes, velocity-gradient directions, and plane-of-sky magnetic-field orientations derived from Planck data for a subsample of well-defined structures. We find that, for cloud structures within our sample, with physical scale $\sim 0.3$ to $\sim 30$ pc, velocity gradients tend to be perpendicular to the major axes, while magnetic-field are generally aligned parallel to them. This scale range differs from those typically probed in studies of dense cores ($\sim 0.05$ pc) and GMC-scale structures ($\gtrsim$ 10 to 100 pc), which have reported scale-dependent variations in relative orientations. In addition, the alignment between velocity gradients and magnetic fields shows a gradual weakening with increasing physical scale. These results suggest that the observed anisotropy of molecular cloud substructures may arise from a combination of large-scale Galactic dynamics, anisotropic gas motions, and magnetic fields, with the relative importance of these effects varying with scale.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes substructures within molecular clouds from the MWISP survey, finding a slight preference for elongation along Galactic longitude (median R=0.96). Velocity gradients are perpendicular to major axes, while magnetic fields align parallel to them. Orientation alignments between velocity gradients and magnetic fields weaken with increasing scale (0.3-30 pc).
AI.motivation: To quantify the geometry and kinematics of molecular cloud substructures at intermediate scales (0.3-30 pc) and understand the interplay between Galactic dynamics, gas motions, and magnetic fields in shaping cloud anisotropy.
AI.method: Substructures were identified from the MWISP survey as spatially connected regions within 20% peak-integrated-intensity contours. Projected morphology was quantified via the scale ratio R=Δb/(Δl·cos b). Relative orientations among structural major axes, velocity-gradient directions, and Planck-derived magnetic fields were analyzed for a subsample.
AI.result: Median R=0.96 (slight elongation along Galactic longitude, stronger at larger scales). Velocity gradients are perpendicular to major axes; magnetic fields are parallel to them. Velocity-gradient–magnetic-field alignment weakens with increasing physical scale over 0.3-30 pc.
AI.conclusion: The observed anisotropy likely results from a combination of large-scale Galactic dynamics, anisotropic gas motions, and magnetic fields, with scale-dependent relative importance.

title: Distinct Gas and Stellar Circular Rotation Curves in the Milky Way Galaxy
comment: The rotation data and python scripts to perform the Grand average and carry out statistical analysis can be found at DOI.org/10.5281/zenodo.20543192
summary: The rotational velocity of interstellar gas in the Milky Way, and other galaxies, has been taken to represent the circular velocity of a test particle in the Galaxy gravitational field, and hence an indicator of the Galaxy mass. The derived circular velocity is found to be too high for the gas to be gravitationally bound to the galaxy given the observed Galaxy mass in stars and gas, and consequently an extra component of mass in the Milky Way and other galaxies, namely dark matter, has been postulated. However recently the observational satellite Gaia, has been carrying out ground-breaking astrometric observations to accurately measure, inter alia, the three dimensional velocities of stars in the vicinity of the Sun and beyond. This has revealed that the circular velocity derived from the stellar population is much less than that of the gas, and the rotation curve, circular velocity versus radius, is distinctly declining with radius, whereas the gas rotation curve is not declining. By combining results from multiple observations of the gas velocity, averaging the velocities in radial bins, we establish that there is a grand average rotation curve. This can be compared directly with a grand average of the published Gaia rotation curves, and the confidence level in the difference between the two estimated by statistical analysis. The difference is shown to have a high degree of confidence, and increases with galactocentric radius. The lower circular rotation curve from the stellar velocities has resulted in significantly reduced estimates of the dark matter mass fraction of the Milky Way. The higher rotation of the gas lacks an explanation, but it is unlikely to be an accurate indicator of the kinematic mass of the Galaxy. This also has significant consequences for the mass of external galaxies based on gas rotation curves.

AI.tldr: Gaia observations show that stellar rotation curves decline with radius, yielding significantly lower circular velocities than those derived from interstellar gas. This difference is statistically significant, increasing with galactocentric radius, challenging the use of gas rotation curves as reliable mass indicators and reducing dark matter fraction estimates for the Milky Way.
AI.motivation: The discrepancy between stellar and gas-derived rotation curves questions the longstanding use of gas velocity as a proxy for gravitational mass, which led to the postulation of dark matter. The authors aim to quantify and statistically validate this difference using Gaia data.
AI.method: Results from multiple gas velocity observations were combined and averaged in radial bins to produce a grand average rotation curve. This was compared to a grand average of published Gaia stellar rotation curves, with statistical analysis estimating confidence levels of the difference as a function of galactocentric radius.
AI.result: The stellar rotation curve is distinctly declining with radius, much lower than the gas rotation curve. The difference is statistically significant, increases with galactocentric radius, and leads to substantially reduced estimates of the Milky Way's dark matter mass fraction.
AI.conclusion: Gas rotation curves are unlikely to be accurate indicators of kinematic mass for the Milky Way, and this finding has significant implications for mass estimates of external galaxies that rely on gas rotation curves.

title: X-ray luminosity function of Compton-thick AGN in the early Universe (z > 3). Robustness and biases of the CTK population
comment: 19 pages, A&A Accepted
summary: The population of Compton-thick (CTK) AGN represents a critical yet elusive phase in the growth of supermassive black holes. Constraining their abundance and evolution at high z is essential for understanding both SMBH growth and the origin of the cosmic X-ray background. We investigate the X-ray luminosity function (XLF) of CTK AGN at z > 3 using one of the largest available samples of X-ray-selected AGN at high z, containing 811 sources from XMM-Newton XXL-N and Chandra CCLS and CDF-S/N surveys. We first selected a subsample of ten high-probability CTK candidates, identified through x-ray spectral fitting. Their multiwavelength properties are examined through SED modelling to assess the robustness of their CTK classification. For most sources, the inferred X-ray luminosities appear overestimated when compared with their IR luminosities. After updating the NH posteriors with IR-informed priors, only three sources remain consistent with the CTK regime. To compute the XLF for the entire CTK AGN population, we used 24 microns photometry to estimate IR luminosities and update the X-ray posteriors for all the remaining sources. Incorporating IR priors systematically reduces the inferred CTK number densities, yielding a more conservative and physically consistent estimate of the XLF. We find that CTK AGN constitute 17 per cent of the total AGN population at 3 < z < 6, consistent with results at lower z. Our analysis reveals no statistically significant evolution in the CTK fraction up to z about 6, suggesting that the most heavily obscured accretion phase remains a persistent component of black hole growth throughout cosmic history. While the overall obscured AGN fraction (NH > 1e23 cm-2) increases toward higher redshifts, the stable CTK fraction supports the interpretation that, at these epochs, the interstellar medium in typical host galaxies cannot produce CTK levels of obscuration.

AI.tldr: Using X-ray and IR data from large high-z AGN samples, this paper finds that Compton-thick AGN constitute ~17% of the AGN population at z>3, with no significant evolution up to z~6, after correcting for IR-informed priors that reduce previously overestimated number densities.
AI.motivation: Compton-thick AGN are a critical but elusive phase in SMBH growth and key contributors to the cosmic X-ray background; their abundance and evolution at high redshift remain poorly constrained.
AI.method: Selected 10 CTK candidates via X-ray spectral fitting from 811 X-ray-selected AGN (XMM-XXL-N, Chandra CCLS, CDF-S/N); used SED modeling and IR (24μm) photometry to update NH posteriors with IR-informed priors; computed XLF with corrected estimates.
AI.result: Only 3/10 candidates remain CTK after IR prior correction; CTK AGN constitute 17% of total AGN at 3<z<6; no significant evolution in CTK fraction up to z~6; overall obscured fraction (NH>1e23) increases with redshift but CTK fraction remains stable.
AI.conclusion: The heavily obscured CTK accretion phase is a persistent component of black hole growth across cosmic history; the stable CTK fraction suggests that typical host galaxy ISM at high z cannot produce CTK-level obscuration.

title: Quenching of Star Formation in Massive Galaxies
comment: 46 pages, 10 figures, plus Supplemental Text (32 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables); Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2026, Vol. 64
summary: The shutdown of star formation - quenching - marks a pivotal transition in the lives of massive galaxies, which dominate the present-day stellar mass density. This review synthesizes our current understanding of the mechanisms that trigger and maintain quiescence. We discuss the nuances of how quiescent systems are identified across cosmic time and summarize the evolving physical properties of the growing massive population, including their stellar populations, chemical enrichment histories, and gas and dust reservoirs, highlighting several key results: (1) Quiescent galaxies can be identified with empirical color selections, but evolving specific star formation rate thresholds offer a more robust physical distinction from star-forming systems. (2) The earliest massive quiescent stellar populations show rapid formation histories and high metallicities, with enhanced $α$-elemental abundances often distinct from local analogs. (3) Nascent studies of gas and dust in quiescent galaxies reveal diverse multiphase reservoirs and outflows, pointing to fast ejective and slow regulatory modes of galaxy quenching. (4) In situ processes establish galaxy central density, while assembly continues via (minor) mergers post-quenching, reshaping all massive galaxies and disrupting rotation in most cases. We distill observations into two broad modes by which massive galaxies form and quench: one involves a rapid, early shutdown driven by supermassive black hole outflows on short timescales; the other proceeds gradually through gas exhaustion, virial heating, or preventative feedback, each leaving distinct observational signatures. Together, these pathways offer a testable framework for modeling the formation and evolution of massive galaxies, which will be informed by future studies of their stars, gas, dust, and dynamics.

AI.tldr: This review synthesizes our understanding of quenching — the shutdown of star formation in massive galaxies — covering identification methods, evolving properties (stellar populations, chemical enrichment, gas/dust), and proposing two broad quenching modes: rapid early shutdown via supermassive black hole outflows versus gradual processes like gas exhaustion, virial heating, or preventative feedback.
AI.motivation: To synthesize current understanding of the mechanisms that trigger and maintain quiescence (shutdown of star formation) in massive galaxies, which dominate the present-day stellar mass density.
