AI.method: A literature review synthesizing observational results on quiescent galaxy identification (color selections, sSFR thresholds), physical properties (stellar populations, chemical enrichment, gas/dust reservoirs), and quenching modes (rapid ejective vs. slow regulatory processes).

(2) Early massive quiescent galaxies have rapid formation, high metallicity, enhanced α-element abundances. (3) Diverse multiphase gas/dust reservoirs and outflows indicate fast ejective and slow regulatory quenching modes. (4) In situ processes set central density; post-quenching minor mergers reshape galaxies and disrupt rotation.

title: Spatially Resolved Nebular-Stellar Reddening with JWST/NIRISS
comment: 17 pages, 19 figures (including appendices), submitted to A&A
summary: An accurate determination of the dust attenuation within galaxies is essential to derive key physical properties such as the star formation rate (SFR). We present an analysis using the JWST/NIRISS data from the GLASS-JWST ERS programme to investigate and characterise the stellar and nebular reddening of galaxies at $1.0<z<2.4$, down to the sub-kpc scale. We use a multiregion fitting method to extract high-quality H$α$ and H$β$ emission line maps for 99 individual galaxies across a stellar mass range $7.0<\log_{10}(M_*/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})<10.5$. We find no evidence for ratios of the Balmer decrement (H$α$/H$β$) below the intrinsic limit for Case B recombination, beyond the expected variation from observational uncertainties. We reproduce the local correlation between the Balmer decrement and total stellar mass, and find no measurable difference when splitting the sample by redshift, with negligible attenuation below $\log_{10}(M_*/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})\lesssim8.5$. Similarly, the best-fit relation between the nebular and continuum reddening follows the same relation as in local starburst galaxies, $E(B-V)_{\mathrm{SED}} = (0.46\pm0.02)E(B-V)_{\mathrm{neb}}$, together indicating no significant evolution in the dust geometry within galaxies out to $z\lesssim2.4$. We derive best-fit linear relations between the differential nebular-stellar reddening and the SED-derived star formation rate (SFR) and stellar mass, finding statistically significant relations for both quantities. We use our spatially-resolved measurements to derive an empirical calibration between the resolved differential reddening, and the SFR surface density. These will enable crucial dust attenuation corrections for spatially-resolved science at higher redshifts where the Balmer lines are inaccessible, such as with future Roman grism observations.

AI.tldr: This paper uses JWST/NIRISS data to analyze dust attenuation in galaxies at z=1.0-2.4 on sub-kpc scales, finding no evolution in dust geometry relative to local relations and deriving empirical calibrations for dust correction at higher redshifts.
AI.motivation: Accurate dust attenuation determination is essential for deriving key physical properties like star formation rate; the paper aims to characterize stellar and nebular reddening in galaxies at intermediate redshifts on spatially resolved scales.
AI.method: Multiregion fitting of JWST/NIRISS data from GLASS-JWST ERS programme to extract Hα and Hβ emission line maps for 99 galaxies (7.0<log₁₀(M*/M☉)<10.5, 1.0<z<2.4), measuring Balmer decrement and comparing nebular vs. continuum reddening.
AI.result: No Balmer decrements below intrinsic Case B recombination limit; local correlation between Balmer decrement and stellar mass reproduced with no redshift evolution; nebular-continuum reddening relation matches local starbursts (E(B-V)_SED = (0.46±0.02)E(B-V)_neb); statistically significant relations found between differential reddening and SFR/stellar mass; empirical calibration between resolved differential reddening and SFR surface density derived.
AI.conclusion: No significant evolution in dust geometry within galaxies out to z≲2.4; derived calibrations enable dust attenuation corrections for spatially-resolved science at higher redshifts where Balmer lines are inaccessible (e.g., future Roman grism observations).

title: Investigating the young stellar populations and hierarchies in nearby galaxies with the UVIT. II. Presenting the properties of ~25,000 UV-detected star-forming clumps
comment: Submitted to ApJS after incorporating referee's comments
summary: Studying young stellar populations within galaxies can help refine our understanding of recent star formation in galaxies and their evolution. With this motivation, we present a catalog of ~25,000 recently formed (within 400 Myr) star-forming clumps (SFCs) in 17 morphologically diverse nearby galaxies, including 8 massive, classic spirals, 6 intermediate-mass, flocculent spirals, and 3 dwarf irregulars. We used far- and near-UV observations from the UltraViolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT), whose ~1.5" angular resolution and 28' field-of-view allow us to probe SFCs at a mean physical scale of ~54 parsec, within the full extent of our galaxies. We adopted a homogeneous SFC detection criterion, corrected for spatially varying dust attenuation (using 6" resolution A_V maps, made by combining FUV with archival infrared observations), and estimated the SFC ages by comparing the observed UV color-magnitude diagrams with Starburst99 simple stellar population models. Using our SFC catalog, we studied the age demographic of the recently formed stellar populations across different galaxy morphologies and observed age trends consistent with several well-known phenomena, such as the inside-out formation of disc galaxies, local gravitational instabilities leading to flocculent spiral arms, and the stochastic nature of star formation in dwarf galaxies. Leveraging full galaxy coverage and FUV data, our catalog complements existing optically-identified star cluster catalogs in the literature towards improving our understanding of star formation across a wide range of galaxy morphologies, masses, and environments. We make the SFC catalog and A_V maps of our 17 galaxies publicly available with this paper.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a catalog of ~25,000 young star-forming clumps (SFCs) within 400 Myr in 17 nearby galaxies of diverse morphologies, using UVIT far- and near-UV observations. It corrects for dust attenuation, estimates ages via UV color-magnitude diagrams and Starburst99 models, and finds age trends consistent with inside-out disk formation, gravitational instabilities in flocculent spirals, and stochastic star formation in dwarfs. The catalog and dust maps are publicly released.
AI.motivation: To improve understanding of recent star formation and galaxy evolution by studying young stellar populations across a wide range of galaxy morphologies, masses, and environments using consistent UV observations.
AI.method: Used UVIT FUV/NUV observations (1.5" resolution, 28' FoV) to detect ~25,000 SFCs in 17 galaxies (8 massive spirals, 6 flocculent spirals, 3 dwarf irregulars). Applied homogeneous detection criteria, corrected for spatially varying dust attenuation using 6" resolution A_V maps from FUV+infrared data, and estimated ages via UV color-magnitude diagrams compared to Starburst99 SSP models.
AI.result: Catalog of ~25,000 SFCs at mean ~54 pc scale; age trends consistent with inside-out disk formation in spirals, gravitational instabilities driving flocculent arms, and stochastic star formation in dwarfs.
AI.conclusion: The UV-based SFC catalog complements existing optical star cluster catalogs and advances understanding of star formation across diverse galaxy types. Public data release includes the SFC catalog and A_V dust maps for all 17 galaxies.

title: Between Degeneracy and Evolution: UV-to-optical Insights into the BH$^*$ Model in Little Red Dots
comment: 22 pages, 15 figures, 4 tables. Submitted for publication in A&A
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are a heterogeneous class of objects, with several proposed scenarios for their physical nature and evolution. While these theories have been tested on individual LRDs using limited spectral features, a systematic Bayesian analysis of the LRD population incorporating the different models across a broad wavelength range is still lacking. In this study, we conduct a consistent ultraviolet (UV)-to-optical continuum fitting analysis of 66 LRDs at 2<z<6 using JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectroscopy. Employing a modified version of Bagpipes--including blackbody (BB) emission affected by Balmer absorption, stellar and nebular emission attenuated by dust, and an active galactic nucleus (AGN) component--we assess the performance of the black hole star (BH*) model in describing the LRD population. We adopt broad priors and therefore do not impose any specific physical scenario. Our results show that only ~6% of LRDs with statistically robust solutions (52 objects in total) are best-fit by a BH* in the optical and a host galaxy in the UV. ~8% of LRDs show BB-dominated optical continua but lack a stellar component or exhibit AGN UV leakage. Most LRDs are dominated by stellar and/or AGN emission in the optical, with minor BB contribution. When we adopt a prior that disfavors a strong AGN continuum to enforce BH*-like solutions, the percentage of BH$^*$ systems increases to ~40%, highlighting the strong degeneracy between a BH* solution and alternative scenarios. Even when BH*-like solutions are enforced, many LRDs still require a stellar-dominated optical continuum. This may reveal limitations of the BH* model or point to an evolutionary sequence in which the BB contribution decreases as the host grows, leading to lower BB temperatures and higher stellar masses at lower z. In this scenario, more pronounced ''V'' shapes would correspond to later stages in LRD evolution.

Only ~6% of LRDs are best-fit by the BH* model (black hole star with Balmer absorption) when using broad priors, while most show stellar/AGN-dominated optical continua. When enforcing BH*-like priors, ~40% fit, revealing strong degeneracies and suggesting potential evolutionary sequences where BB contribution decreases as hosts grow.
AI.motivation: Existing LRD classification schemes rely on limited spectral features without systematic Bayesian population-level analysis. A consistent framework comparing multiple physical models across UV-to-optical wavelengths is needed to resolve the physical nature and evolution of LRDs.
AI.method: Modified Bagpipes spectral fitting with five components: blackbody (BB) with Balmer absorption, stellar emission, nebular emission with dust attenuation, and AGN continuum. Bayesian inference with broad priors applied to 66 LRDs at 2<z<6 using JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectroscopy. Additional test using priors that disfavor strong AGN to enforce BH*-like solutions.

Most LRDs are stellar/AGN-dominated in optical with minor BB contribution. Enforcing BH*-like priors raises BH* fraction to ~40%, demonstrating strong model degeneracy. Even then, many require stellar-dominated optical continuum.
AI.conclusion: The BH* model has limited descriptive power for most LRDs under unbiased priors. Strong degeneracies exist between BH* and alternative scenarios. The results suggest a potential evolutionary sequence where BB contribution decreases with host growth, leading to lower BB temperatures and higher stellar masses at lower redshift, with pronounced "V" shapes representing later evolutionary stages.
